title: Behar: hold him before he falls (Leviticus 25:35)
hook: support a struggling neighbor before he falls; Maimonides calls this the highest giving

segments.voice: Yesterday: ona'at devarim, wronging with words. Your line was words can wrong. Did you feel the gap open before a sharp reply, and step into it? Day four hundred twenty-four.

Picture a donkey on a dirt road with a heavy sack on its back. The sack starts to slip. One person walking alongside can put a hand on it and push it back into place. Easy. Now let it fall. It's in the dust, split open, grain everywhere, and five people together can barely heave it up again. That picture comes from an old rabbinic commentary on a single verse in this week's portion. It isn't about donkeys. It's about the moment a neighbor's life starts to slip.
screen: `A SACK STARTS TO SLIP.` → `ONE HAND CAN HOLD IT.` → `ONCE IT FALLS, FIVE CAN'T.`

segments.voice: Leviticus twenty-five, verse thirty-five, still in Behar. If your brother grows poor and his means begin to fail beside you, "then thou shalt uphold him". In Hebrew, v'hechezakta bo: take hold of him, strengthen him. The ancient commentary called the Sifra, and Rashi after it, read the verb with care. It doesn't say lift him up off the ground. It says hold him, which only works while he's still standing. That's where the donkey comes from. Catch the load while it's slipping, because once it's down, it takes a crowd. In the twelfth century, Moses Maimonides wrote out eight levels of giving to the poor, from the giver who gives grudgingly at the bottom to the very top. And the top rung isn't the biggest donation, or even the anonymous one. It's this verse. Strengthen someone before they need to ask: a gift, a loan, a partnership, or finding them work, so they can stand on their own. He quotes thou shalt uphold him as the proof. Look at what that does to charity. The highest form isn't a rescue. It's prevention. It happens quietly, before anyone has to stand in a line or fill out a form or say the hard words, I need help. It keeps a person's dignity whole, and it keeps them a neighbor instead of turning them into a case. The verse goes on: let him live with thee. Not beneath you. With you.
screen: `THEN THOU SHALT UPHOLD HIM.` · `HOLD WHAT'S STILL STANDING.` · `MAIMONIDES: THE TOP RUNG.` · `PREVENTION, NOT RESCUE.` · then, large: `LET HIM LIVE WITH THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help someone before they fall. Settle, and breathe. Let faces come to mind: a friend who's gone quiet, a coworker whose hours were cut, a relative carrying more than they say. Don't rush past anyone. Notice whose load seems to be slipping. Then think of one small way to put a hand on the sack: an introduction, a ride, a meal, a lead on a job, a message that says I noticed. Hold that person in mind until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Behar, the portion on the mountain. Its last great teaching: strengthen a neighbor while they're still standing. The next portion begins tomorrow.
Your line: hold him before he falls. Today, do the one small thing you thought of, before anyone has to ask. Day four hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Jewish communities run free-loan societies, job networks and quiet support funds rooted in this verse; Maimonides' eight levels of giving, from the Mishneh Torah's laws of gifts to the poor, are widely taught, with helping someone become self-supporting at the top.

myth: for Maimonides, the highest giving is the largest gift
the top rung is strengthening someone so they don't need to ask: a loan, a partnership, a job.
the commentary compares a struggling neighbor to a slipping load
hold it while it slips; once it falls, it takes many hands.

fork.setup: a friend's business is wobbling. they haven't asked for anything. what does Maimonides put at the top of the ladder of giving?
options: wait until they ask, then give generously.
help now, with a loan, partnership or work, so they stay standing.
fork.reveal: the highest level, in Gifts to the Poor 10:7, is strengthening someone before they fall, so they never need to ask. he cites "thou shalt uphold him."

original.note: Hebrew: and you shall uphold him. from chazak, strong: strengthen him.

trapdoor: what you thought: charity means giving to people who've already lost everything.
what it means: the verse asks you to hold a neighbor up while they're still standing.
what a scholar hears: Maimonides, Gifts to the Poor 10:7, puts this verse at the top of his eight levels of tzedakah.

sources.ref: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Gifts to the Poor 10:7–14

notes: 'then thou shalt uphold him' from JPS 1917 Leviticus 25:35, from memory; please confirm. 'let him live with thee' is given as paraphrase of the verse's end (JPS: 'as a stranger and a settler shall he live with thee'); confirm the phrasing is acceptable.
The donkey-load image is Rashi on 25:35, from the Sifra. Rashi says one person can hold it while on the donkey, and five cannot raise it once fallen; confirm.
Maimonides placed in the twelfth century (Mishneh Torah completed c. 1180).
Maimonides' eighth (highest) level: gift, loan, partnership, or finding work; confirm the list.
